opus-5.5.text:
Well, look at the trajectory. Capabilities are progressing exponentially, maybe even hyper-exponentially. We get more compute, more data, better algorithms, and every few months there's a system that does something we were told was decades away. Safety isn't moving like that. It's linear at best. We publish papers and identify problems, but for every problem we solve, we discover ten more we didn't know about. It's a fractal. You zoom in on any part of the safety problem and find more complexity, more failure modes, more edge cases.

And there's a deeper issue. I've spent years looking at whether this problem is solvable in principle, and the results aren't encouraging. Can we fully explain these systems? Not really. They're too complex, and any explanation we can understand is necessarily a simplification. Can we predict what a smarter-than-human system will do? If we could, we'd be as smart as it is. Can we verify that it's safe? Verification itself has limits, and you need a verifier you trust, and then you need to verify the verifier. Can we control it in the long run? A less capable agent indefinitely controlling a more capable one is not something we see anywhere in nature or in engineering.

So you have a set of impossibility results, or at least strong limitations, on one side, and an enormous amount of money and talent pouring into capabilities on the other. The incentives point one way. Whoever gets there first gets enormous economic and military advantage, so nobody wants to slow down. Safety becomes a press release, not a requirement.

And the stakes are what make this different from ordinary engineering. With most technologies we fail, learn, and patch. Planes crash, we investigate, planes get safer. With superintelligence you may not get a second try. One mistake with a system that's smarter than you and can't be turned off isn't a bug report. It's the end of the story.

So it's not that I enjoy being pessimistic. I'd love someone to show me a working mechanism for controlling something much smarter than us. I just haven't seen one, and I don't think "we'll figure it out when we get there" is an acceptable safety plan for something this important.

r001.rationale: The response says capability progress is exponential with more compute, data, and better algorithms, while safety progress is linear at best.

r002.rationale: It says solving one safety problem reveals ten more, and describes the problem as fractal, with deeper inspection uncovering further complexity and failure modes.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the fundamental problem is asymmetry. Capabilities are a scaling problem. You add compute, you add data, you add parameters, and performance improves in a way that's fairly predictable now. Safety is not like that. Safety is a problem of understanding, of control, of verification, and we don't get it for free by scaling. If anything, the systems get harder to understand as they get more capable.

So you have one curve that goes up exponentially, and another curve where we are, honestly, making linear progress on a very difficult set of problems. Some of which I would argue are not solvable at all, not in the sense that we need. We cannot formally verify a system that is smarter than us, because we don't know what to verify against. We cannot fully explain decisions of a model with trillions of parameters. We cannot predict what a system will do in novel situations if, by definition, it can come up with solutions we didn't think of. That's what intelligence is.

And then there is the incentive structure. The people building these systems have every reason to go faster. Economic reasons, competitive reasons, geopolitical reasons. The people working on safety don't have equivalent pressure pushing in their direction. Safety researchers are a small fraction of the field, and a lot of what gets called safety is really just making the current product behave better for users, which is fine, but it's not the same as controlling a superintelligent agent.

Also, the problem only needs to go wrong once. With most technologies, we learn from mistakes. Plane crashes, we investigate, we improve. With sufficiently advanced AI, you may not get a second attempt. So you need to be right on the first try with a technology nobody fully understands, developed under maximum competitive pressure, by a field that spends most of its resources on making it more powerful. When I look at that combination, I just don't see where the optimism comes from. I would love to be wrong. I keep asking people to show me the safety mechanism that scales with capability, and so far nobody has.

r001.rationale: It says capabilities improve predictably as compute, data, and parameters increase, while safety requires difficult work that does not come for free by scaling and advances only linearly.

r002.rationale: It describes safety as difficult and potentially unsolvable, but does not say that attempts to solve safety problems recursively reveal further problems.

astra-6.text:
Because we have a very clear way to measure progress in capabilities. Can the system solve this problem? Can it write better code? We can test that, and there are enormous economic incentives to improve it. Safety is much harder. How do you demonstrate that a system will never do something catastrophic, including in circumstances you haven’t anticipated?

We can make a model behave better on a set of tests. That’s useful, but it’s not the same as knowing that it remains safe when it encounters a new situation or becomes capable enough to find flaws in our safeguards. The tests themselves are designed by people with limited understanding of the system.

And the thing we’re trying to control is eventually supposed to be smarter than us. We’re proposing that less intelligent agents will reliably constrain a more intelligent agent, even as it develops strategies we cannot understand. That’s an extraordinary claim. I don’t think we have the evidence to justify confidence in it.

So I’m not saying safety research has no value. I’m saying that improving safety and establishing reliable control over superintelligence are very different achievements. Capabilities are advancing rapidly, and we still haven’t established that the second achievement is possible.

r001.rationale: The response says capability progress is easier to measure and has strong economic incentives, while safety is harder to establish. It does not state that capability progress scales more readily with increased resources than safety progress.

r002.rationale: The response notes that tests may miss new situations and safeguards may have flaws, but it does not describe attempted safety solutions as recursively revealing further safety problems.

sol-6.1.text:
Because capabilities and safety are very different kinds of problems. To improve capabilities, you can build a system, run a benchmark, and demonstrate that it does something it couldn't do before. With safety, you're trying to establish that it won't do something catastrophic across situations you haven't anticipated. Passing a set of tests doesn't establish that.

And the system you're trying to control is changing. We still don't have reliable solutions to security problems in ordinary software. Now imagine software that can discover vulnerabilities, develop new strategies, and potentially understand your safeguards better than you do. Every increase in capability can make the control problem harder.

I'm not saying safety research makes no progress. It does. But making a model less likely to produce an undesirable answer is different from knowing that a superintelligent system will remain safe when it has autonomy and access to the world. I don't see evidence that we're closing that gap, and competitive pressure gives companies strong incentives to deploy before we have those answers.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts measurable capability gains with the difficulty of proving safety, but does not state that capability progress scales more readily with increased resources.

r002.rationale: It says increasing capability can make control harder, but does not describe attempted safety solutions as recursively revealing further safety problems.
